newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel zealots head out to spread revolution.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel zealots head out to spread revolution.

text.p: Two hundred rebel zealots headed south on Monday to preach a gospel of revolution against President Mobutu Sese Seko in the last two Zairean towns to fall into their hands.
The "teachers" flew from rebel headquarters in Goma to the cities of Lubumbashi and Mbuji-Mayi as part of a rebel drive to re-educate populations under their control.
The teachers are schooled at the General Commissariat for Information and Propaganda in the ideology of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL).
Despite their mission, some of them are suprisingly frank.
"Now we are going to Lubumbashi to brainwash or open the eyes of the people and show them what to do to get rid of the spirit of Mobutism," Esperance Uwimana, a former secretary, told Reuters.
Teachers receive free accommodation and are paid one dollar a day for the work expected to last around one month and a bonus of about $100. Some said they were taking their families.
Lubumbashi, Zaire's second largest city, fell to the AFDL last Wednesday and Mbuji-Mayi, Zaire's diamond capital, was seized on April 5. The rebels hold nearly half of Africa's third largest country.
The rebels led by Laurent Kabila are fighting to oust Mobutu after 32 years in power and rid Zaire of his political class.
The AFDL "Programme of Political Ideology" is 10 three-hour seminars. At its core is a simple message in lesson four: "The principal goal of the revolution is the conquest of power."
Other lessons are on civil liberty, reasons for the failure of a revolt in 1964-65 and definitions of the "true" soldier and "true" army, compared with Mobutu's notoriously ill-disciplined troops.
Critics argue it smacks of indoctrination, a term often used by its teachers, and say residents are coerced to participate.

They point to the course's Marxist-sounding rhetoric and say the roots of Kabila's Popular Revolutionary Party lie in the leftist nationalism of Zaire's first prime minister Patrice Lumumba, who was murdered in 1961.
"It is a socialist philosophy in the sense of respect for the citizens and a division of the spoils of the state among all the citizens," said Frederic Ilunga N'Goy, head of a parastatal.
International mining companies are keen to exploit Zaire's great mineral wealth under Kabila's rule. The rebels are re-negotiating contracts signed under the Mobutu government.
Kabila denies he has an authoritarian agenda for Zaire. He says the AFDL holds elections in most towns it seizes and wants general elections after a one-year transitional period.
"First we must liberate the country and then all parties will be free to contest future elections," he said recently.

"The ideology of the Alliance is to give everybody his place, to let everybody do as they please. I am going to Lubumbashi not as a foreigner but as a brother or a sister to make the Congolese see they must be united," Uwimana said.
At the heart of the AFDL's ideology is a drive against corruption. Under Mobutu's rule, the word "kleptocracy" was coined to describe the venal way the country was governed.
"We were all Mobutists so we were all living on bribes, even me. If somebody tells you different they are lying. We were so badly paid we were forced to live like that," Ilunga said.
